text:
Norman Swan: Hello, and welcome to the Health Report with me, Norman
Swan. Today a special feature from Hagar Cohen on a very important issue for
many parents: it's stillbirths. They can be reduced and are preventable, as was
shown on a recent Background Briefing by Hagar Cohen. But what Hagar has
also found is that when stillbirths occur, there may be unacceptable variation in
how they are dealt with by hospitals. Some of the statements and descriptions
you'll hear in this program could be disturbing, but it is an important issue. Here's
Hagar Cohen's feature:

Hagar Cohen: It was early in the morning that Karen Anderson, a professional
photographer, received an urgent text from the hospital.

Karen Anderson: We are off to the Mater at Saint Leonards. I received a call to
say that there had been a stillbirth and to come in and take some photographs for
the family.

Hagar Cohen: Karen is a volunteer with the Heartfelt Foundation. They
photograph families that have experienced premature births or have children with
terminal illnesses or, like in this instance, a stillbirth. It's not a job for the
fainthearted.

Karen Anderson: Some babies have…their skin has torn during birth, or they
had passed away in utero a little while ago so their skin is not very well.

Hagar Cohen: Not all stillborn babies look like this. Karen was told that the
stillborn baby this morning looks perfect.

Karen Anderson: Yes, exactly. Some babies look exactly perfect. Their skin is
perfect and it's hard to realise that the baby has passed away. It just doesn't
seem to be for any reason.

Hagar Cohen: Karen says parents usually feel apprehensive posing with their
dead baby, but she says later they are glad they did it.

Karen Anderson: It must be quite confronting to say to a family, you know,
'Would you like someone to come in and take photographs of your baby?' But I
think even through that grief, a lot of parents realise that they may not have any
memories if nobody has taken any photographs, and to have a professional
 
come in and take photographs that they could sometimes even put up on their
wall if they wanted to, I think it's just very important.

Hagar Cohen: Arriving at the Mater hospital, Karen is greeted by social worker
Deb de Wilde. It's the third time they've met in 10 days. There's been a rush of
stillborns, almost like a cluster.

Deb de Wilde: Yes, I guess you could describe it as a cluster, though I don't
know that using that term in the medical or epidemiological sense is actually
accurate. But yes, in that sense I guess you could say a cluster.

Hagar Cohen: The family at the Mater today are sending time with their baby
Chloe. It's a practice that is encouraged by many hospitals, and parents Hanh
and Matt have opted to stay and look after baby Chloe at the hospital for seven
days. This may seem unusual, and for Hanh and Matt this experience is full of
unknowns. But Deb de Wilde, a social worker with over 30 years experience,
guides them along the process.

Today, the day before the funeral, Hanh and Matt are debating whether Chloe
should stay overnight for a sleepover.

Hanh: We're leaning against the sleepover because tomorrow is such a big day
that if we don't sleep, tomorrow we're not actually going to be very…

Deb de Wilde: Okay, so we might revisit the temazepam idea or…?

Hanh: No, no, I'm just worried that if you don't get enough sleep, everything is
hyper, and her last day is not…

Deb de Wilde: …you just do what you…I'll do what you tell me.

Hanh: So we are thinking, Deb, maybe we have her now, then take a break,
have her after dinner and then put her in from, say, 11 until 6.

Hagar Cohen: Chloe was stillborn six days ago and since then Hanh and Matt
have been looking after her like any other parent would, dressing her, bathing
her, and once they even took for a walk.
 
Matt: So we got to take Chloe out to a nearby garden, just a little quiet, private
one and just sort of hang out with her, show her the sunshine I guess, the
flowers, fresh air. That has been pretty special. If we are going to have Chloe
with us for a week, it feels a bit strange to not change her clothes. We would
change our clothes, right?

Hanh: Yes, and to us she is alive…well, she is not alive, but to us she is our
baby, so she is going to have all of the things that all babies should have, aren't
you my darling? Yes. Yes. Do you want to touch her?

Hagar Cohen: Yes.

Hanh: You can touch her.

Hagar Cohen: Chloe is cold to touch, and that's because she goes in and out of
a fridge.

Hanh: You are super, super cold little Chloe, super cold today. That's good, that
means you can stay out and hang out longer.

Hagar Cohen: Mother Hanh had a textbook pregnancy and she still doesn't know
why Chloe died.

Hanh: She was born on Saturday night and she had her autopsy on Tuesday,
Wednesday.

Hagar Cohen: Do get answers?

Hanh: Not yet.

Matt: Not yet.

Hanh: I think it will be a while. But whether we get her autopsy now or in three
months, it doesn't matter, it doesn't change the outcome.

Hagar Cohen: The outcome—having a stillborn—is something that no one
prepares for. So it was the social worker Deb de Wilde who talked them through
what they could do with the baby.
 
Matt: We had no idea, we had no idea, and then she just slowly and in great
comfort…makes us feel very relaxed about it I guess, and all these things you
just don't think about, like obviously the funeral process, but everything from can
we go outside, can we hold her, can we change her, can we take her home or
can we…

Hanh: She throws options at you that you don't even think are possible, like do
you know that you could take her home tonight?

Matt: Or we could have her here overnight in a little cot. I can only hope this sort
of things happens in not just private hospitals but public and everywhere,
because if it didn't, I've got to feel for those parents.

Hanh: If other parents don't get this, what do they do?

Vita: That was just absolutely horrific to me and my mind just shut down and I
just went I have to get out of here. I just wanted to get out of there and…yeah, it
was horrific. And I felt in that moment that our baby belonged to the hospital and
it wasn't my baby. Obviously they saw him as a specimen, and that's how he was
presented to us.

Hagar Cohen: This mum's experience shows that while some parents are given
the golden standard, others are exposed to so much apathy and carelessness
that it traumatises them for life. Vita, who gave birth at Westmead hospital in
Sydney, spent only a few minutes with her stillborn baby, Frankie James.

Did you get to touch Frankie?

Vita: I touched the caul I think briefly when he was still in the caul, but no I didn't,
no.

Hagar Cohen: And that's your biggest regret?

Vita: Yes, my biggest regret is that I didn't spend that precious time with him.
Even though he had passed away and it was a scary situation, he was still my
baby and that was the only chance I got to see his little body and I missed it.

Hagar Cohen: We'll hear more from Vita later in the program. But across
Australia, six babies are stillborn every day. The care and support for their
 
parents in some hospitals is often neglected. To draw attention to this, the
Stillbirth Foundation has commissioned a study to assess the economic impact of
stillbirth to our health system. The Stillbirth Foundation is an organisation that
funds research into stillbirth, and most of its funding comes from bereaved
parents. Foundation president Victorian Bowring says that the study, which is
due to be released in October, has found stillbirth is costing the economy
millions.

Victoria Bowring: It will be in the hundreds of millions. Stillbirth is not just an
issue that needs to be dealt with by the families who experience it, it's an issue
that we should all be concerned about. The cost to the families, to society is
enormous and long term, and some families never recover from the financial
burden that stillbirth has, which is just an added trauma that goes with the
tragedy of the loss of their child. It's indicative of how it's quite a compounding
loss, and hopefully through indicating that there is a financial burden associated
with stillbirth for the economy, we may be able to get government to take it more
seriously.

Hagar Cohen: Over the past few years, Victorian Bowring says she has lobbied
health departments to prioritise training for hospital staff. She says it has been a
fruitless exercise and there has been very little investment from government in
this area. An economic impact study into stillbirth may seem cold, but Victoria
says she feels it's a pragmatic way to make people stand up and listen. She
wants to suggest that an investment now is a cost saving in the long run.

Victoria Bowring: It's sad that we live in a time where to be able to exhibit a cost
of something gives greater leverage in having it dealt with. But it's the reality of
the way things work, and sometimes we need to work with that in order to get the
result that we need.

Hagar Cohen: The result we need is not only a better service at the hospital but
also better follow-up care when the parents return home. Researchers from
Sydney University and the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital interviewed 35 mothers
after stillbirth. They found a high level of dissatisfaction.

Diana Bond: I'm talking about nine tertiary hospitals in the Sydney area, so not
just one centre but generally we found that the follow-up care was such that
 
families were seen sporadically. Some families slipped through the cracks and
were not seen.

Hagar Cohen: Diana Bond is the researcher with the Sydney stillbirth study who
interviewed the mums. She said that many of them felt the clinicians they got in
their follow-up appointments were careless.

Diana Bond: Often they were seen by a clinician that they had not met before.
Very often it might have been a junior registrar or somebody who was not familiar
with their history. So they felt…they were often seen in antenatal clinic, which
meant that they were surrounded by pregnant women and had to wait a long
time, and they found that very confronting. It's very traumatising for them to go
back to that clinic which was a scene of their pregnancy and it brought back a lot
of traumatic memories. And the appointments were often rushed. A lot of the
results that they wanted to hear about were not there. They had to repeat their
story and explain why they were there. So it was not ideal for them, they found it
actually quite traumatising.

Hagar Cohen: Can you give me an example?

Diana Bond: I remember somebody received a home visit from a midwife who
was not aware of their situation and walked in the door and said, 'And so how's
the baby doing?' And it took a while before she realised that the baby had died.

Hagar Cohen: Not all parents experience of this kind of treatment. The Sydney
stillbirth study found that some parents were looked after by sensitive clinicians,
and others were being let down and traumatised. To address this problem Diana
Bond convinced the RPA to lend them a space for a special clinic that would look
after parents six weeks after a stillbirth. But no one would fund it. So the local
RSL stepped in.

Diana Bond: We're so grateful to the Canterbury Park RSL for funding the clinic.
After the stillbirth study our dream was to start this clinic, and we realised it was
absolutely just such a necessary part of care. The hospital at the time were
gracious in providing us a room, and the Canterbury RSL were looking for a
project to support and they provided seed funding for two years.
 
Hagar Cohen: This clinic, called Integrated Support After Infant Loss, or ISAIL,
opened last year, and already has 60 parents on their books. Julia, whose
daughter Anna was stillborn at 20 weeks, is one of them.

Julia: So Diana Bond from the ISAIL clinic contacted me on a Friday night, and
we spoke for a while, and then she booked in an appointment to meet us, like a
debrief. So I had written 101 questions that I wanted to ask, and I really felt like
they gave us as much time as we needed.

Hagar Cohen: For an hour and a half Julia's obstetrician and her midwife
discussed all of those questions. All Julia wanted to know; was her daughter's
death preventable?

Julia: If I had have gone private could this have changed, if I had have gone to
hospital sooner could this have changed…?

Hagar Cohen: So you wanted to know if it was preventable.

Julia: Yes basically, if it was preventable. And, you know, the doctor that I saw at
the medical centre on that Monday morning, did she misinform me?

Hagar Cohen: Julia's loss was the most traumatic event in her life, but she feels
supported. That's not what happened to Vita, who plunged into a black hole after
the birth and death of her first son Frankie James.

Vita: And I went into a very dark depression after that and it was a real struggle.

Hagar Cohen: Vita's partner Peter was worried.

Peter: For quite some time she was barely leaving the house. I'd sometimes get
home from work and she wouldn't have had anything to eat or drink all day, and I
was like, oh boy, it's pretty serious.

Hagar Cohen: Peter and Vita now live with their two babies. In 2012 when Vita
was pregnant with Frankie she was over the moon. But at the 19-week scan she
discovered he had died.

Vita: And I remember I was lying on the table and the lady doing the ultrasound,
her face kind of froze and she seemed to be taking quite a long time. And then
 
she said, 'I just have to check something,' and she left the room, and then she
came back with another person who said, 'I'm sorry, but your baby's heart isn't
beating.' They left the room and I remember I just screamed like an animal.

Hagar Cohen: Baby Frankie died at the point where it's still considered a
miscarriage, just. So Vita was told to wait for her body to miscarry at home. She
was scared.

Vita: I was terrified. When I came out of the shock I realised I've got this dead
baby inside me and I've got to get it out somehow, now. It was just a horrible
thought, to think that my womb had become a tomb.

Hagar Cohen: After three days at home waiting, still no miscarriage. So Vita
went to the hospital.

Vita: And I had an amniocentesis done, which is where they put a needle into the
tummy and extract the fluid around the baby to test it. And I remember I went into
that room and lay down and there were two doctors talking about their
weekend…I was crying and they were saying, 'Now, now, stop crying, you can
have another one, don't cry.' And I just felt bereft. I felt like I was being difficult by
being upset. They couldn't understand why I was sad.

Hagar Cohen: Three days later, with still no miscarriage, Vita decided to give
birth to Frankie. Her labour was painful and lasted 16 hours.

Vita: At one stage one of the hospital midwives came in and she seemed quite
annoyed with me and she said, 'You know there are women here having live
babies and it's not all about you.'

Hagar Cohen: Another midwife who took over Vita's care was lovely but
inexperienced. She started her shift when Vita was asleep after having an
epidural.

Vita: And then I remember her coming in and tapping me on the shoulder and
waking me up and saying, 'I'm just going to check to see how you are
progressing,' and she lifted up the covers and exposed my legs and she
screamed and jumped backwards and said, 'Oh, it's happened.' She was
absolutely horrified and terrified and surprised.
 
Hagar Cohen: Because the baby had come out and no one knew?

Vita: Yes. I didn't even know. It was just there in between my knees. And she
said, 'Wait there, don't touch, don't look at it, don't look at it, don't look.' And she
went out of the room.

Hagar Cohen: The midwife ran out to call for some help. She came back with an
obstetrician.

Vita: He I think lifted our little son up and showed him to us for like 10 seconds, it
was a very short amount of time. He was actually inside the caul, so he was
inside the amniotic sac, it hadn't burst. And I thought he was incredibly beautiful
and magical, to see this sac surrounding him was quite a miracle really. And then
the obstetrician took him away.

Hagar Cohen: Vita says from then on everything happened very quickly.

Vita: I remember kind of going what just happened, where has he taken him. A
while later he came back and he had burst the sac and our baby was sitting in a
metal kidney dish, like an organ, and he brought him back in this kidney dish and
took a pen out of his pocket and he kind of poked him with the pen and was
pointing out this is where the umbilical cord is and…yeah, he was trying to
explain what all the bits were to us in front of us, but again, in a very insensitive
manner, in a kidney dish with his pen.

Hagar Cohen: Frankie James was born at 19 weeks and six days, officially he
was a miscarriage, one day short of a stillbirth. That meant no birth certificate, no
death certificate. Officially he didn't exist. Nor was a Heartfelt photographer
called.

Vita: I asked for photos and we were given three photos which were taken with a
flash and they were just horrible, like post-mortem type photos.

Hagar Cohen: So they didn't call a photographer, you know, like from the
Heartfelt Foundation?

Vita: No, and I didn't know about that and I wish I had known. I would have loved
to have had that service, that would have been wonderful. I didn't know about it.
And the photos that we have, I can't stand to look at them, they're awful.
 
Hagar Cohen: Vita and Peter left hospital on the day Frankie James was born.
They spent only a few moments with him. What happened at Westmead is
exactly what social worker Deb de Wilde would like to prevent. She explains to
parents who are usually in shock that they can spend time and touch their baby.

Deb de Wilde: There's nothing particularly new about this approach, it's just
legitimising it within a hospital. I think we have many cultural black holes in our
society, and one of them is around death, and particularly the death of a child.
That's why the people I see have no cultural reference point, and no inner
knowledge to guide them about what they should think or feel or do. And that's
why sometimes you need a wise older presence to perhaps slow things down
long enough so that people can get to a point where they know for themselves
what they need to do around that little baby.

Hagar Cohen: Deb's relationship with parents usually starts just after they are
told that their baby has died.

Deb de Wilde: So, often I guess the most usual scenario from me would be just
knocking on a delivery suite store and walking into a room to see people who are
often either extraordinarily distressed, tearful, angry, but most often composed,
incredulous, disbelieving. So then sometimes it's just trying to backtrack a little bit
and explain my role and to say to them in effect that, look, I'm going to see them
quite a lot over their time in hospital and that I am going to do everything I can to
make this situation bearable.

Hagar Cohen: And with these words Deb de Wilde first introduced herself to
Katrina. Katrina was 39 weeks pregnant when she arrived at the hospital with
what she thought were normal contractions. But she was wrong. She had had a
placental abruption, which is when the placenta comes away from the wall of the
uterus and the baby's supply of blood stops. She'd lost a lot of blood, and was
about to be anaesthetised for an emergency caesarean. Doctors told her the
baby was dead. On top of that, Katrina was scared she was going to die.

Katrina: But what was going through my mind at that point was literally just that I
had absolutely no control over my body, over my life, and that I had to just
completely submit and surrender myself and trust that these people would look
after me, and if they couldn't then this was how I was going to die. And I could
 
feel gushing happening again and again, and I was worried that I was losing all
my blood. And I became aware that an anaesthetist was telling me that he was
about to put me to sleep, and one of his nurses was preparing the mask over my
face to help me go off to sleep. But just before all that there was a lady who
introduced herself over the top of my head, and I couldn't see her but I could hear
her, and she said, 'My name is Deb and I'm a social worker, and I'm going to see
you when you wake up.' And for me to hear that at the very last minute before I
was put to sleep did give me some hope that I would wake up.

Hagar Cohen: Katrina did wake up knowing her baby had died and she was in a
lot of pain. At the hospital she was looked after in the gynaecology ward.

Katrina: So I don't think that the gynaecology nurses knew how to broach the
subject of my stillborn baby. They didn't ever voluntarily initiate any conversation
about it, they didn't ever offer to arrange to have the baby brought to me. It's
almost like they consciously avoided talking about Lydia for fear that it would
upset me. And obviously I was tremendously upset and at this point after having
two days for the information that she was stillborn to sink in and the acute phase
of my c-section resolving, I was feeling able to experience more emotional pain
about it. And oftentimes I would be visibly upset and in tears, crying for her, and I
feel that they said some quite insensitive things.

Hagar Cohen: Like what?

Katrina: One of the nurses told me that I should stop worrying because I'll have
another one.

Hagar Cohen: Another baby?

Katrina: Yes. And I didn't say anything but I felt like, gosh, at this point I don't
actually know if I can have another baby, how dare you say that, that doesn't
make me feel better at all. At this point I didn't want another baby, I just wanted
Lydia.

Hagar Cohen: The social worker Deb de Wilde saw this and suggested Katrina
moves to the maternity ward where spending time with a stillborn baby is
accepted.
 
Katrina: Deb's approach is very central to the baby that you've lost. And she
validates the baby that you've lost, she makes really beautiful comments and
remarks about the baby that you've lost, and the focus is all about that baby. And
she gives you compliments on how you are being a beautiful mum to your baby,
irrespective of whether it's alive or dead. And that made me feel so much better
because I felt like I was getting that chance to be Lydia's mum and I was having
the opportunity to demonstrate how I would have been her mother had she lived.

Hagar Cohen: Katrina's last night with Lydia was precious.

Katrina: So I stayed up very late with her in my room, and tried to squeeze a
lifetime of being her mum into 12 hours. So I held her a lot, just tried to remember
the weight of her, the size of her, the look of her, the feel of her in my arms. And I
played some DVDs, I read her stories, and I told her stories about her mum and
dad. And I flipped through a photo album with her and I played music to her in
the morning so that I could associate the memory of her being with me with
particular songs.

Hagar Cohen: Lydia was buried the next day. Katrina is grateful to have met Deb
de Wilde because she knows not all parents are given the opportunity to care for
their stillborn. And this is the crux of the problem, says Victoria Bowring from the
Stillbirth Foundation. The support for bereaved parents is a neglected area. The
service parents get is a question of luck.

Victoria Bowring: But it's very much dependent on the maternity unit itself and
the midwives that are working in the various hospitals. There's very little in the
way of formal training around stillbirth for midwives and nursing staff in the
hospitals.

Hagar Cohen: She says this kind of training is urgent, and she can't understand
why this isn't recognised.

Victoria Bowring: We fight very hard to have it added to the national health
agenda, but up until now we've not been terribly successful in maintaining that or
getting the government to actually take it on board.

Norman Swan: That special Health Report on stillbirths and how they are dealt
with by hospitals was prepared by Hagar Cohen, with assistance from Joel
 
Werner. We approached Westmead Hospital for a response to the program, and
they claimed that they do follow guidelines for dealing with both miscarriages and
stillbirths, and they do it in a humane way, and they also claimed that there is no
record of a complaint by the family in question.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report. I look forward to your
company next week.

Hanh: She was born on Saturday night and she had her autopsy on Tuesday,

Hanh: Not yet.

Matt: Not yet.

Hanh: I think it will be a while. But whether we get her autopsy now or in three

Matt: We had no idea, we had no idea, and then she just slowly and in great

Hanh: She throws options at you that you don't even think are possible, like do

Matt: Or we could have her here overnight in a little cot. I can only hope this sort

Vita: That was just absolutely horrific to me and my mind just shut down and I
just went I have to get out of here. I just wanted to get out of there and…yeah, it
was horrific. And I felt in that moment that our baby belonged to the hospital and

presented to us.

Vita: I touched the caul I think briefly when he was still in the caul, but no I didn't,
no.

Hagar Cohen: And that's your biggest regret?

Vita: Yes, my biggest regret is that I didn't spend that precious time with him.
Even though he had passed away and it was a scary situation, he was still my
baby and that was the only chance I got to see his little body and I missed it.

Hagar Cohen: We'll hear more from Vita later in the program. But across
Australia, six babies are stillborn every day. The care and support for their

parents in some hospitals is often neglected. To draw attention to this, the
Stillbirth Foundation has commissioned a study to assess the economic impact of
stillbirth to our health system. The Stillbirth Foundation is an organisation that
funds research into stillbirth, and most of its funding comes from bereaved
parents. Foundation president Victorian Bowring says that the study, which is
due to be released in October, has found stillbirth is costing the economy
millions.

Victoria Bowring: It will be in the hundreds of millions. Stillbirth is not just an
issue that needs to be dealt with by the families who experience it, it's an issue
that we should all be concerned about. The cost to the families, to society is
enormous and long term, and some families never recover from the financial
burden that stillbirth has, which is just an added trauma that goes with the
tragedy of the loss of their child. It's indicative of how it's quite a compounding
loss, and hopefully through indicating that there is a financial burden associated
with stillbirth for the economy, we may be able to get government to take it more
seriously.

Hagar Cohen: Over the past few years, Victorian Bowring says she has lobbied
health departments to prioritise training for hospital staff. She says it has been a
fruitless exercise and there has been very little investment from government in
this area. An economic impact study into stillbirth may seem cold, but Victoria
says she feels it's a pragmatic way to make people stand up and listen. She
wants to suggest that an investment now is a cost saving in the long run.

Victoria Bowring: It's sad that we live in a time where to be able to exhibit a cost
of something gives greater leverage in having it dealt with. But it's the reality of
the way things work, and sometimes we need to work with that in order to get the
result that we need.

Hagar Cohen: The result we need is not only a better service at the hospital but
also better follow-up care when the parents return home. Researchers from
Sydney University and the Royal Prince Alfred Hospital interviewed 35 mothers
after stillbirth. They found a high level of dissatisfaction.

Diana Bond: I'm talking about nine tertiary hospitals in the Sydney area, so not
just one centre but generally we found that the follow-up care was such that

families were seen sporadically. Some families slipped through the cracks and
were not seen.

Hagar Cohen: Diana Bond is the researcher with the Sydney stillbirth study who
interviewed the mums. She said that many of them felt the clinicians they got in
their follow-up appointments were careless.

Diana Bond: Often they were seen by a clinician that they had not met before.
Very often it might have been a junior registrar or somebody who was not familiar
with their history. So they felt…they were often seen in antenatal clinic, which
meant that they were surrounded by pregnant women and had to wait a long
time, and they found that very confronting. It's very traumatising for them to go
back to that clinic which was a scene of their pregnancy and it brought back a lot
of traumatic memories. And the appointments were often rushed. A lot of the
results that they wanted to hear about were not there. They had to repeat their
story and explain why they were there. So it was not ideal for them, they found it
actually quite traumatising.

Hagar Cohen: Can you give me an example?

Diana Bond: I remember somebody received a home visit from a midwife who
was not aware of their situation and walked in the door and said, 'And so how's
the baby doing?' And it took a while before she realised that the baby had died.

Hagar Cohen: Not all parents experience of this kind of treatment. The Sydney
stillbirth study found that some parents were looked after by sensitive clinicians,
and others were being let down and traumatised. To address this problem Diana
Bond convinced the RPA to lend them a space for a special clinic that would look
after parents six weeks after a stillbirth. But no one would fund it. So the local
RSL stepped in.

Diana Bond: We're so grateful to the Canterbury Park RSL for funding the clinic.
After the stillbirth study our dream was to start this clinic, and we realised it was
absolutely just such a necessary part of care. The hospital at the time were
gracious in providing us a room, and the Canterbury RSL were looking for a
project to support and they provided seed funding for two years.

Hagar Cohen: This clinic, called Integrated Support After Infant Loss, or ISAIL,
opened last year, and already has 60 parents on their books. Julia, whose
daughter Anna was stillborn at 20 weeks, is one of them.

Julia: So Diana Bond from the ISAIL clinic contacted me on a Friday night, and
we spoke for a while, and then she booked in an appointment to meet us, like a
debrief. So I had written 101 questions that I wanted to ask, and I really felt like
they gave us as much time as we needed.

Hagar Cohen: For an hour and a half Julia's obstetrician and her midwife
discussed all of those questions. All Julia wanted to know; was her daughter's
death preventable?

Julia: If I had have gone private could this have changed, if I had have gone to
hospital sooner could this have changed…?

Hagar Cohen: So you wanted to know if it was preventable.

Julia: Yes basically, if it was preventable. And, you know, the doctor that I saw at
the medical centre on that Monday morning, did she misinform me?

Hagar Cohen: Julia's loss was the most traumatic event in her life, but she feels
supported. That's not what happened to Vita, who plunged into a black hole after
the birth and death of her first son Frankie James.

Vita: And I went into a very dark depression after that and it was a real struggle.

Hagar Cohen: Vita's partner Peter was worried.

Peter: For quite some time she was barely leaving the house. I'd sometimes get
home from work and she wouldn't have had anything to eat or drink all day, and I
was like, oh boy, it's pretty serious.

Hagar Cohen: Peter and Vita now live with their two babies. In 2012 when Vita
was pregnant with Frankie she was over the moon. But at the 19-week scan she
discovered he had died.

Vita: And I remember I was lying on the table and the lady doing the ultrasound,
her face kind of froze and she seemed to be taking quite a long time. And then

she said, 'I just have to check something,' and she left the room, and then she
came back with another person who said, 'I'm sorry, but your baby's heart isn't
beating.' They left the room and I remember I just screamed like an animal.

Hagar Cohen: Baby Frankie died at the point where it's still considered a
miscarriage, just. So Vita was told to wait for her body to miscarry at home. She
was scared.

Vita: I was terrified. When I came out of the shock I realised I've got this dead
baby inside me and I've got to get it out somehow, now. It was just a horrible
thought, to think that my womb had become a tomb.

Hagar Cohen: After three days at home waiting, still no miscarriage. So Vita
went to the hospital.

Vita: And I had an amniocentesis done, which is where they put a needle into the
tummy and extract the fluid around the baby to test it. And I remember I went into
that room and lay down and there were two doctors talking about their
weekend…I was crying and they were saying, 'Now, now, stop crying, you can
have another one, don't cry.' And I just felt bereft. I felt like I was being difficult by
being upset. They couldn't understand why I was sad.

Hagar Cohen: Three days later, with still no miscarriage, Vita decided to give
birth to Frankie. Her labour was painful and lasted 16 hours.

Vita: At one stage one of the hospital midwives came in and she seemed quite
annoyed with me and she said, 'You know there are women here having live
babies and it's not all about you.'

Hagar Cohen: Another midwife who took over Vita's care was lovely but
inexperienced. She started her shift when Vita was asleep after having an
epidural.

Vita: And then I remember her coming in and tapping me on the shoulder and
waking me up and saying, 'I'm just going to check to see how you are
progressing,' and she lifted up the covers and exposed my legs and she
screamed and jumped backwards and said, 'Oh, it's happened.' She was
absolutely horrified and terrified and surprised.

Hagar Cohen: Because the baby had come out and no one knew?

Vita: Yes. I didn't even know. It was just there in between my knees. And she
said, 'Wait there, don't touch, don't look at it, don't look at it, don't look.' And she
went out of the room.

Hagar Cohen: The midwife ran out to call for some help. She came back with an
obstetrician.

Vita: He I think lifted our little son up and showed him to us for like 10 seconds, it
was a very short amount of time. He was actually inside the caul, so he was
inside the amniotic sac, it hadn't burst. And I thought he was incredibly beautiful
and magical, to see this sac surrounding him was quite a miracle really. And then
the obstetrician took him away.

Hagar Cohen: Vita says from then on everything happened very quickly.

Vita: I remember kind of going what just happened, where has he taken him. A
while later he came back and he had burst the sac and our baby was sitting in a
metal kidney dish, like an organ, and he brought him back in this kidney dish and
took a pen out of his pocket and he kind of poked him with the pen and was
pointing out this is where the umbilical cord is and…yeah, he was trying to
explain what all the bits were to us in front of us, but again, in a very insensitive
manner, in a kidney dish with his pen.

Hagar Cohen: Frankie James was born at 19 weeks and six days, officially he
was a miscarriage, one day short of a stillbirth. That meant no birth certificate, no
death certificate. Officially he didn't exist. Nor was a Heartfelt photographer
called.

Vita: I asked for photos and we were given three photos which were taken with a
flash and they were just horrible, like post-mortem type photos.

Hagar Cohen: So they didn't call a photographer, you know, like from the
Heartfelt Foundation?

Vita: No, and I didn't know about that and I wish I had known. I would have loved
to have had that service, that would have been wonderful. I didn't know about it.
And the photos that we have, I can't stand to look at them, they're awful.

Hagar Cohen: Vita and Peter left hospital on the day Frankie James was born.
They spent only a few moments with him. What happened at Westmead is
exactly what social worker Deb de Wilde would like to prevent. She explains to
parents who are usually in shock that they can spend time and touch their baby.

Deb de Wilde: There's nothing particularly new about this approach, it's just
legitimising it within a hospital. I think we have many cultural black holes in our
society, and one of them is around death, and particularly the death of a child.
That's why the people I see have no cultural reference point, and no inner
knowledge to guide them about what they should think or feel or do. And that's
why sometimes you need a wise older presence to perhaps slow things down
long enough so that people can get to a point where they know for themselves
what they need to do around that little baby.

Hagar Cohen: Deb's relationship with parents usually starts just after they are
told that their baby has died.

Deb de Wilde: So, often I guess the most usual scenario from me would be just
knocking on a delivery suite store and walking into a room to see people who are
often either extraordinarily distressed, tearful, angry, but most often composed,
incredulous, disbelieving. So then sometimes it's just trying to backtrack a little bit
and explain my role and to say to them in effect that, look, I'm going to see them
quite a lot over their time in hospital and that I am going to do everything I can to
make this situation bearable.

Hagar Cohen: And with these words Deb de Wilde first introduced herself to
Katrina. Katrina was 39 weeks pregnant when she arrived at the hospital with
what she thought were normal contractions. But she was wrong. She had had a
placental abruption, which is when the placenta comes away from the wall of the
uterus and the baby's supply of blood stops. She'd lost a lot of blood, and was
about to be anaesthetised for an emergency caesarean. Doctors told her the
baby was dead. On top of that, Katrina was scared she was going to die.

Katrina: But what was going through my mind at that point was literally just that I
had absolutely no control over my body, over my life, and that I had to just
completely submit and surrender myself and trust that these people would look
after me, and if they couldn't then this was how I was going to die. And I could

feel gushing happening again and again, and I was worried that I was losing all
my blood. And I became aware that an anaesthetist was telling me that he was
about to put me to sleep, and one of his nurses was preparing the mask over my
face to help me go off to sleep. But just before all that there was a lady who
introduced herself over the top of my head, and I couldn't see her but I could hear
her, and she said, 'My name is Deb and I'm a social worker, and I'm going to see
you when you wake up.' And for me to hear that at the very last minute before I
was put to sleep did give me some hope that I would wake up.

Hagar Cohen: Katrina did wake up knowing her baby had died and she was in a
lot of pain. At the hospital she was looked after in the gynaecology ward.

Katrina: So I don't think that the gynaecology nurses knew how to broach the
subject of my stillborn baby. They didn't ever voluntarily initiate any conversation
about it, they didn't ever offer to arrange to have the baby brought to me. It's
almost like they consciously avoided talking about Lydia for fear that it would
upset me. And obviously I was tremendously upset and at this point after having
two days for the information that she was stillborn to sink in and the acute phase
of my c-section resolving, I was feeling able to experience more emotional pain
about it. And oftentimes I would be visibly upset and in tears, crying for her, and I
feel that they said some quite insensitive things.

Hagar Cohen: Like what?

Katrina: One of the nurses told me that I should stop worrying because I'll have
another one.

Hagar Cohen: Another baby?

Katrina: Yes. And I didn't say anything but I felt like, gosh, at this point I don't
actually know if I can have another baby, how dare you say that, that doesn't
make me feel better at all. At this point I didn't want another baby, I just wanted
Lydia.

Hagar Cohen: The social worker Deb de Wilde saw this and suggested Katrina
moves to the maternity ward where spending time with a stillborn baby is
accepted.

Katrina: Deb's approach is very central to the baby that you've lost. And she
validates the baby that you've lost, she makes really beautiful comments and
remarks about the baby that you've lost, and the focus is all about that baby. And
she gives you compliments on how you are being a beautiful mum to your baby,
irrespective of whether it's alive or dead. And that made me feel so much better
because I felt like I was getting that chance to be Lydia's mum and I was having
the opportunity to demonstrate how I would have been her mother had she lived.

Hagar Cohen: Katrina's last night with Lydia was precious.

Katrina: So I stayed up very late with her in my room, and tried to squeeze a
lifetime of being her mum into 12 hours. So I held her a lot, just tried to remember
the weight of her, the size of her, the look of her, the feel of her in my arms. And I
played some DVDs, I read her stories, and I told her stories about her mum and
dad. And I flipped through a photo album with her and I played music to her in
the morning so that I could associate the memory of her being with me with
particular songs.

Hagar Cohen: Lydia was buried the next day. Katrina is grateful to have met Deb
de Wilde because she knows not all parents are given the opportunity to care for
their stillborn. And this is the crux of the problem, says Victoria Bowring from the
Stillbirth Foundation. The support for bereaved parents is a neglected area. The
service parents get is a question of luck.

Victoria Bowring: But it's very much dependent on the maternity unit itself and
the midwives that are working in the various hospitals. There's very little in the
way of formal training around stillbirth for midwives and nursing staff in the
hospitals.

Hagar Cohen: She says this kind of training is urgent, and she can't understand
why this isn't recognised.

Victoria Bowring: We fight very hard to have it added to the national health
agenda, but up until now we've not been terribly successful in maintaining that or
getting the government to actually take it on board.

Norman Swan: That special Health Report on stillbirths and how they are dealt
with by hospitals was prepared by Hagar Cohen, with assistance from Joel

Werner. We approached Westmead Hospital for a response to the program, and
they claimed that they do follow guidelines for dealing with both miscarriages and
stillbirths, and they do it in a humane way, and they also claimed that there is no
record of a complaint by the family in question.

I'm Norman Swan, this has been the Health Report. I look forward to your
company next week.
